strengths: First non-asymptotic complexity analysis of AIS without log-concavity assumptions, using novel proof techniques with Girsanov theorem and optimal transport
Innovative use of action integral (metric derivative) as complexity measure, avoiding restrictive isoperimetric assumptions
Unified analytical framework connecting JE, AIS, and RDS through path measure analysis
Identifies limitations of geometric interpolation via Prop. 9 and proposes RDS-based alternative
Technically sound proofs with sophisticated handling of path measure discrepancies and KL divergence bounds
weaknesses: Complete absence of experimental validation—no numerical experiments validating bounds, comparing algorithms, or demonstrating practical utility

RDS methodology incomplete: Theorem 11 provides framework only; end-to-end complexity depends on external results (Huang et al. 2024) which themselves have exponential ε-dependence for score estimation
Limited novelty in some components: JE analysis builds on Guo et al. (2025); TI complexity known from prior work; proof techniques are somewhat standard in the optimal transport literature
Presentation density with heavy notation (Õ, Θ̃) and complex multi-term bounds that make it difficult to extract actionable insights or understand when different terms dominate

strengths: Technically sound non-asymptotic oracle complexity analysis leveraging Girsanov theorem and optimal transport without explicit isoperimetric assumptions
Novel action-based complexity framework unifying continuous-time (JE) and discrete-time (AIS) analysis through KL divergence minimization
Extends prior results beyond log-concave distributions to broader classes satisfying mild smoothness conditions
Unified treatment of multiple methods (JE, AIS, RDS) with clear algorithmic instantiations and complexity relationships
Interesting observation about inefficiency of geometric interpolation via exponential lower bound on action (Proposition 9)
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Complete absence of experiments—no numerical validation of bounds, no empirical comparison of methods, no investigation of tightness, no ablation studies. For a methods paper at a top conference, this is disqualifying.

Significant gap between theory and practice: complexity bounds involve multiple terms (d³/²/ε², mβA_r^{1/2}/ε², dβ²A_r²/ε⁴) whose dominance is unclear; no guidance on method selection for practitioners
Action-dependent bounds lack practical guidance: action A is problem-dependent and not directly controllable by algorithm designer; only limited characterization of when curves have small action

RDS analysis is incomplete: Theorem 11 provides a framework but defers concrete complexity to other works; score estimation bottleneck (Section E.5) shows all methods require strong assumptions or exponential complexity

No lower bounds to establish optimality: Proposition 9 only lower bounds action for one specific case; cannot assess tightness of main results. The ε⁻⁴ dependence in discretization error term seems loose without justification.

Limited novelty: problem is decades old; main contribution is refined analysis rather than new insights or methods. Improvements over log-concave settings not quantified. Incremental progression JE→AIS→RDS follows naturally.

Geometric interpolation critique insufficient: Proposition 9 addresses only one structured case (symmetric Gaussian mixture); doesn't broadly characterize when geometric interpolation fails. Real-world applicability unclear.

Dense presentation obscuring key insights: notation heavy (Õ hides logs; multiple subscripts); interdependencies between terms not clearly explained; crucial proofs relegated to 46-page appendix making main text hard to verify

Incomplete analysis of key bottlenecks: score estimation for RDS is essential yet complex (involves another optimization problem); trade-off between curve properties and drift estimation difficulty not resolved
Theory-practice gap on key parameters: β-smoothness and second moment m are assumed known but difficult to estimate; dependence on these quantities may be loose in practice

strengths: First rigorous non-asymptotic complexity analysis for AIS without requiring log-concavity assumptions, significantly extending prior work limited to strongly log-concave distributions

Novel proof technique using Girsanov theorem and optimal transport that characterizes complexity via action of probability measure curves, avoiding explicit isoperimetric assumptions and providing interpretable bounds
Comprehensive theoretical framework unifying Jarzynski equality, AIS, and reverse diffusion samplers with clear conceptual connections (e.g., TI as special case of AIS)
Concrete complexity bounds with meaningful dependence on problem parameters: O(dβ²A²/ε⁴) for JE and Õ(d³/²/ε² ∨ mβA_r^{1/2}/ε² ∨ dβ²A_r²/ε⁴) for AIS
Identification of practical limitations through Proposition 9 showing exponential lower bound on action for geometric interpolation of Gaussian mixtures
Rigorous and technically sound proofs with careful treatment of measure-theoretic details and appropriate use of advanced tools (backward stochastic integrals, Girsanov theorem)
Detailed algorithms provided with explicit update rules for reproducibility
weaknesses: Complete absence of numerical experiments is a critical gap—no empirical validation of theoretical bounds, no demonstration of tightness, and no guidance on when bounds are practically informative
No matching lower bounds provided; tightness of bounds remains open, so unclear whether ε⁴ dependence and other complexity factors are fundamental or artifacts of the proof technique

Assumption 2 still requires finding an approximate stationary point with ||x*|| ≤ 1/√β, which while addressed by optimization remarks, adds unaccounted complexity and may be restrictive for some problems

RDS algorithm has limited practical applicability: Theorem 11 provides only a framework with actual complexity deferred to existing work, and Section E.5 reveals pessimistic complexities (exponential in dimension or other parameters) that make RDS inferior to AIS

Limited practical guidance on when each complexity term dominates in Theorem 8, how to efficiently estimate action A a priori, or clear scenarios where practitioners should prefer one method over another
Proof techniques, while novel in application, build substantially on Vargas et al. (2024) and standard optimal transport results; the conceptual advance is meaningful but incremental
Geometric interpolation limitation (Proposition 9) is specific to Gaussian mixture case; general implications for other interpolation schemes unclear
Extensive use of Õ notation hides potentially large logarithmic factors that could be significant in practice

strengths: First non-asymptotic analysis of AIS without log-concavity assumptions, using novel action-based framework from optimal transport that weakens isoperimetry requirements
Technically sophisticated with rigorous integration of Girsanov theorem, forward-backward SDEs, and Wasserstein-2 metric derivative in novel ways
Multiple algorithmic contributions: analysis of continuous JE (Thm. 2), first oracle complexity for discrete AIS (Thm. 4), and principled RDS-based algorithm (Thm. 5)
Insightful negative result (Prop. 1) providing exponential lower bound on geometric interpolation action, offering quantitative explanation of mass teleportation phenomenon
Clean methodological contribution: elegant decomposition of path measure KL divergences that is generalizable and provides new perspectives on variance reduction
Comprehensive treatment with well-structured progression from theory to algorithms, supported by extensive appendix with complete proofs and supplementary lemmas
weaknesses: Tightness of bounds unknown (acknowledged by authors): unclear whether ε-dependence in Theorems 2 and 4 are tight, limiting confidence in claimed complexity characterizations

Limited practical guidance despite theoretical sophistication: 'action' is theoretically natural but practitioners given no guidance on how to estimate or use it; authors acknowledge practical interpretability 'not well understood'

Experimental validation insufficient: only 2D demonstrations (Modified Müller Brown, 4-component Gaussian mixture); no high-dimensional validation; no ablation studies; missing comparison matrix with other multimodal methods
Gap between lower and upper bounds: Prop. 1 lower bound on geometric interpolation doesn't directly imply exponential time requirement; unclear what practitioners should extract from this result

RDS complexity concerning: proposed methods still have dimension-dependent complexity (e.g., SNDMC: O((β(m² ∨ d)/ε)^O(d))), partially defeating purpose of removing log-concavity; unclear when RDS is preferable to AIS
Action of OU process (Prop. 2) still dimension-dependent (O(dβ + m²)): limited evidence that OU curve provides clear separation from geometric interpolation for general high-dimensional distributions
Missing analysis of score estimation: Section E.5 reviews four different RDS variants but provides no principled guidance on which to use when; connection to overall complexity unclear

strengths: First non-asymptotic complexity analysis of AIS without log-concavity assumptions—a meaningful theoretical advance
Elegant use of action (Wasserstein metric derivative) instead of isoperimetric inequalities—more generally applicable framework
Technically sound proofs leveraging Girsanov theorem and optimal transport rigorously
Comprehensive treatment covering continuous dynamics (JE), discretization (AIS), and algorithmic proposals (RDS)
Explicit quantification of action cost for geometric interpolation (Prop. 1), clearly motivating limitations of standard methods
weaknesses: Limited proof novelty: heavily builds on Guo et al. (2025) for sampling; extension to normalizing constant estimation via different KL thresholds feels incremental rather than fundamentally novel

Incomplete RDS analysis: Theorem 5 only provides framework; delegates actual complexity to four external methods (RDMC, RSDMC, ZODMC, SNDMC) with incomparable bounds and different assumptions
Severe practicality gap: bounds depend on unknowable constants (m, β, A, d); action A is difficult to compute or bound a priori; for Gaussian mixture with m=10, bounds become useless (A ≳ 10^13)
Weak experimental validation: only 2D experiments, no comparison with recent methods, large variances in results (AIS: ±7.67 on Gaussian mixture), hyperparameter tuning opaque
Lower bound on action doesn't imply exponential convergence time for JE (acknowledged page 10), undermining motivation for RDS over improved geometric interpolation
Focuses exclusively on geometric interpolation λ(θ) = 2β(1-θ)^r; claims of generality overstated given restricted setting in Theorem 4
Action concept lacks practical interpretability: no guidance on how to estimate or bound A for specific problems; circular dependence on curve choice πθ
